utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning to you, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, yesterday, Mr. Groome asked you a question with respect to who had bought the bottle of brandy that you drank from in Pionirska Street, and if I understood your answer correctly, it was the following: That it was the bottle that you had brought and that you consider that in your conversation, you did not say that Mujo had gone to buy it but that you had, in your statement. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, you said that you think that that is what it said in your statement when it was written down. I should like to read a portion of that statement of the 17th of November in B/C/S, which I believe is the original. So could you tell me whether that is what you were thinking of when you said it, and it is page 78 of the B/C/S version and it says the following, your words: A No, I only went, took the alcohol, the alcohol I drank with Mujo and that neighbour of his. I don't know his name. I wasn't, um, carrying anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: That means that you brought it. The witnesses say yes.

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: The question was the bottle.

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked Mujo were we going to have a drink. "Yes," he said, "let's", and I went and bought.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I seem to feel that you said yesterday that he went to buy it.

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I did. On the basis of that, it emerges that you bought the bottle, but if I understand it correctly, you didn't buy it then but previously earlier on and you had the bottle already; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In answering a question with respect to the time you spent in hospital, on two -- twice you talked about your transfer to the neurosurgery department; is that correct or were you thinking of neuropsychiatry?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, I was thinking about neuropsychiatry, the neuropsychiatric ward because when I had operated my spine in Zemun, I was at the neurosurgical department. But this was in Uzice, and as far as I know, there isn't a neurosurgical department in Uzice. It was the neuropsychiatric ward.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you answered the question from Mr. Groome with respect to some photographs or pictures or drawings, you said that often, some patients would stick a picture of a horse up above your bed and that this was a joke, a practical joke. Does that mean that all of them knew that you had broken your leg falling off a horse or was it for some other reason?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They all knew, everybody knew, and they were making practical jokes. It was -- they were joking because they had nothing better to do. They had a lot of time on their hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: May I remind you both to pause, please. You are stretching the interpreters with the speed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Vasiljevic, talking about (redacted) and your explanation and answer in response to Mr. Groome's question regarding some sort of written document which the witnesses are mentioning, have mentioned, you answered, but I'd like to confirm this again to see whether that was precise, whether you remember at all having written this certificate, this kind of certificate, because you said that if it existed at all, it might have been a telephone number and address. Did I understand that to be your answer to Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I couldn't have written any other kind of certificate for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Groome also asked you whether (redacted) knew your address in view of the fact that, according to what you said during your testimony, he kept passing by your house. Now, my question for you is this: Did he ever come into your house and did he know your telephone number or did you ever talk over the phone with him?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think they had the telephone. I don't think so. I'm certain, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, Mr. Groome asked you about cleaning the town. Now, do you consider that the sanction or punishment towards you was instead of serving a prison sentence, you were told to clean the town? Actually, you said yes to that question. Now, the question is: Did anybody tell you at all that you were punished in any way? Did they give you a document stating that or was the cleaning of the town a work assignment or had your prison sentence been reverted to this town-cleaning punishment?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a work obligation, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: A work obligation in fact.

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Although they didn't say they wouldn't lock me up. Well, later on, I broke my leg, so perhaps I would have problems if I didn't want to go up to the line, front line. They had other problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Groome asked you how you dared to report the case in Sase to the chief of police, Tomic, and were you not afraid of the consequences. Now, did you have trust and confidence in the then-chief Tomic to tell him something that might have jeopardised you or was something else the case? Was it because of something else?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tomic was the chief of police. I trusted him. And we're neighbours. We live close by. We're not next-door neighbours, but we do live close by. We lived in the same street.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, talking about the things you were accused of, the singing of songs for which you and some others were sentenced, can you remember the actual judgement for these convictions? Were you singing one song or more than one song? What did it say in the judgement?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One song. That's what it says in the judgement, one song.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Was it just one line or several verses?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was just a short song, perhaps ten words to the song.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And what about the other case, the -- you said that you had come into conflict with a neighbour because of your sister, that she was the cause, but I think that it would be a good idea if you explain to us what had actually happened to your sister, that is to say, what had caused your reaction to this neighbour in connection with your sister?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the neighbour always made problems. He was always going to court for one thing or another. He would provoke and insult and joke with my sister. I am the father -- I and my father cautioned him, but he wouldn't listen. And I was convicted to four months in prison and one year parole.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So this was a conditional sentence, meaning that you would go to prison for four months if you were to repeat that act?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and one year parole.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: But you never repeated that kind of act, did you? So that conditional sentence was never applied and put into effect, was it?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Groome also asked you and said that he considered that you were the only, or almost only, person who knew that the people were from Koritnik in Pionirska Street. My question is: As you had heard -- as you have heard in the course of these proceedings that the people passed the Rvez bridge going up to Visegrad Hotel, and then from the Visegrad Hotel back across the Rvez bridge taking the Uzice road to Pionirska Street and into Pionirska Street, was that the centre, the actual centre of town? Were there lots of people living there? And how many people could have seen this movement?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, but do you mean in town or in Pionirska Street? When you say "the centre of town," are you thinking of Pionirska Street or some other locality?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I'm thinking about their movement from the Visegrad Hotel, through town, across the Rvez bridge to Pionirska Street and the entrance into Pionirska Street, which if I'm right, goes from the main street -- main road leading to Uzice.

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there could have been quite a number of people. It was town, buildings all round, the urban area, and they were in the police station, as far as I understood, and then went to the hotel where the police was and to the Red Cross. That's where they -- the direction they pointed them to, as they said. And then Pionirska and the school, there were soldiers up there. The army was close by. And I didn't know where they were. They were in the house, as you saw, by the road. It's quite wrong that I was the only one who could have known.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Asked by Mr. Groome about the horse that you went to fetch and what you were going to do with it, what your intentions were, you said that you felt like having a ride, riding the horse, and then that you were going to release him and point him in the direction which you mentioned. Now, my question for you is the following, in concrete terms: Did you like horses and riding that much, and did you not perhaps want to keep the horse a little while longer and be able to ride it before you released it, before you let it go?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me explain this to you. I liked horses when I was a child, and my house had horses, and I had a horse. And I fell off the horse and was in hospital, hitting my head when I was in eighth form. I would earn for my books and for my -- the books and the textbooks that my sisters used. And my father bought some tar, buying tar. And I liked horses. I always liked horses. And it was very difficult for me when my father sold our horse. I loved that horse. And I wouldn't change it for any other animal, especially a good horse.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yesterday, Mr. Vasiljevic, I think you said that in Visegrad, at the time, that there were two imams or hodzas as you called it. "Hodza" is the other name for "imam"; is that correct? Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Where did they live, in town or out of town?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In town, right by the Panos restaurant, in the centre. Or more precisely, from the post office under the Panos restaurant there was a warehouse, and they had the Islamic religious house there and they lived there. I know both of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did any of them have a horse, either one of them?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They lived in town. I don't think they had a horse.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: As far as you know, were you alive -- were they alive? Sorry. Did you hear that anything had happened to them?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't hear that anything had happened to them, and I'm quite sure that they are alive today. People would have heard about it, because they're hodzas, religious leaders. People would have known. He was the main man for religion. And as -- a witness said that, but that can be checked out. There's no problem. It's no problem. One of them was younger; one of them was older. So somebody would have said if something had happened to any of them. One was 65 years old. The other might have been about 50.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You may return -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, just one bit of confusion. If I could just inquire of Mr. Domazet, he referred to page 78 of a B/C/S transcript. Was he referring to the 16th, the interview of the 16th or the interview of the 17th?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unless I got muddled, the B/C/S page is 78. It should be the 17th. It doesn't say on the page, however, but as it refers to the conversation and interview of the previous day, that it was on the second day.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, I'd -- if I may ask a single question to Mr. Vasiljevic to clear up what I believe is a confusion on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Why? It's a matter of re-examination. You raised the issue about it. You can tender the statement or it has been tendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It has been tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: What is the point of all this?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Just to clear it up for the Court for clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Re-examination is re-examination. Mr. Vasiljevic, you may return to your seat behind your counsel. Oh, I'm sorry, my colleagues wish to ask some questions. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, I would like to bring you back to the situation which was described by VG81. You said you know her for many years. She says she knows you for many years, and you say you recognise her immediately when she entered the room here. This situation happened on May 18, 1992, and it's at transcript page 1.220, line 18. I will read it what she -- to you what she said: "I went with my family to Kosovo Polje with the intention to work on the land. I was carrying basket with some seeds. At the entrance at the gate of the Mr. Vasiljevic's house, there stood Mitar with his wife and three unknown uniform individuals. Mitar Vasiljevic approach us and he wanted my ID card, identity card. He kept my identity card and he told me, and I quote, she said, 'Don't let me look for you,' and it happened about noon on 18th of May." My question is: If such an incident happened, why you wanted her ID card if you know her for 15 years? And my second question is: What you have done with this ID card?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Judge, individual 81 I know excellently. I know her very well. She lived while -- before she was married, she lived in my neighbourhood one kilometre away. I also know her husband, and I'm wondering she thought this up. Now, why would I need her identity card, a woman that I know well. I know her brother. I know her family well. I have known her for years. I worked in the -- in restaurants. She worked in the municipality building, and would come and have breakfast in the restaurant. I knew her very well. I would like it if her husband came to testify about that, perhaps she'll convince him, but I'd like to hear his statement. I'd like his opinion. I'd like him to state his opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: So do you understand well that this situation happened, you were standing in front of your entrance with your wife, and she was passing, because you said with her husband, she said with her family here, but you didn't ask her for ID card. Do you understand well?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I didn't see her. I don't remember having seen her. That's not true. None of it's true. I didn't see her there. That's what she says. I didn't see her, and my wife will testify and say the same thing, I'm sure. And even if I had seen her, why would I ask for her identity card when I know her?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: So you are stating that this situation didn't happen; is that okay?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Judge, just like the other things that she's been saying. She says she saw me from the 14th to the 25th, and I was in hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Can you tell me, Mr. Vasiljevic, what is the profession of Mr. Lukic? You are waiter. What is his profession, Milan Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milan Lukic, I think, completed secondary school for plumbing, for plumbing, plumbing secondary school, but I don't think he ever worked as a plumber. He didn't actually work at all. Now, whether he worked in Serbia, perhaps he did for a short time. I know he worked in Switzerland, that he had a cafe there of some sort, but he didn't do -- he didn't follow his profession, what he was trained to do, and then from Switzerland he came back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: So can you estimate for the Chamber that this sort of education is done at 18 or what age he finished his studies?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The school lasts 11 years, which means exactly 18. We start school at 7 and we finish school at 18, that is, secondary school. And a trade means 8 years of primary school and 3 of trade makes it 11 years of schooling. You need 11 years of schooling. That's that secondary level schooling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: And you said that you were no possibility to socialise with him, that he left soon, he was working in Obrenovac, Switzerland, Germany or some other places and you also said that there was an age difference between you and him, and all this meant that he wasn't present at the Visegrad municipality, is that true, for many years?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite certainly, he wasn't there. After school, he went to the army for 15 months, and he never worked again there, but if he came back from Switzerland for his holidays, that was for brief periods. I don't remember seeing him. Mostly, I knew him when he was a child at school. We sort of saw each other then, but not afterwards, and I'm 13 years older. I think he was born in 1967.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: So am I right if I conclude that he wasn't present in the area for 6 years? Because I think I remember 1992 he was 24.

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, thereabouts, 24. He wasn't much older than 24.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: But after all those years of absence in the area, it must have been very difficult for him to know who is who, and which house belongs to whom. My question is: Did Milan Lukic ask you to give him information about people and ownership of the houses concerning the ethnicity of the people? That's one question. The second question is: Did you ever give him such information, information voluntarily?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me see. As far as this area downstream is concerned, he knows well which are the Muslim villages and which are the Serb villages. He has many friends from school there, and we all know which are the Muslim and which are the Serb villages. Whether he knew in town which are the Muslim or Serb houses, he probably didn't, but I don't think he made any selection. All he cared about was that somebody was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: So coming back to my question or questions, did he ask you to give him information about the people and the houses concerning the ownership? That's my question. Please answer yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. He never asked me to tell him, never.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: And did you ever give him at least single information concerning this point voluntarily, without asking?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: I would like to bring your attention to the VG14 who stated here on the 13th of September, and it's transcript page 436, line 7, and I will read it for you, and he, VG, stated that on 7th of June, when they were driven in the direction of Sase, so you were approaching the Drina River in the cars in the direction of Sase, "Mitar Vasiljevic, when they stopped near the house, said to Milan Lukic, and I quote what he said, 'That this was a Muslim house.'" Did you say this, and if yes, why?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milan Lukic knew which were the Muslim and which were the Serb houses, and the house that is shown on the photograph is not a Muslim house. It's a Serb house. Kosoric is the surname. Stojan is his first name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: You know, I'm not familiar with the area, but the witness VG14 said when you stopped, you told to Milan Lukic that this is a Muslim house. That is in his statement.

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the car stopped -- I couldn't have said that. I wasn't with Milan in the car. He said that in -- that there were six people in the Yugo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: With him in the car -- you were not in the car with Milan Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in the Yugo, with Meho Dzafic, the second car, another car.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: And my last question -- thank you for this. And my last question is: Evidence which was presented in this case suggested that Mr. Gavrilovic had an official function in the SDS, Srpska Democratic Stranka. You also mentioned that after the funeral of your cousin, you reported back to Mr. Gavrilovic in Uzamnica and begged not to be imprisoned any more. My question is: Is Mr. Gavrilovic, who you reported to, the same person as the one who has an official function in Serbian Democratic Party?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the same person, only I apologise if I said that I addressed him in Zemunica [sic]. He was at the command in Bikavac. I was in the prison in Uzamnica. So if I said I spoke to him in Uzaminica, please correct that. That's wrong. He was working in the command, and the command was up there at the hotel in Bikavac. So if I said that I addressed in Uzaminica, I should like to correct that. That's wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Thank you. And to your knowledge, what function did Mr. Gavrilovic have in the SDS? Is his first name Dragan?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know him as Drago. It's probably Dragan or Dragomir, but I know him as Drago. He was influential, and later on, I think he was president of the SDS party. Not at the beginning of the war. It was Branimir Savovic who was president, and later on it was him. I don't know when he took over that duty. Maybe it was in 1994 or 1995, but I'm not sure. But I do know that for a time he was president of the party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Yes. He was influential in the party. Thank you. And another question is --

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: -- did he give you the task of cleaning the street? Was it him who gave you this task?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He told me. We went to school together, so he said, "Organise cleaning of the town," and I agreed, and that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: And in what function did you -- did he give you this task? He was your commander?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He wasn't the main commander. He did have a position in the army at some higher level. What duty exactly he had, I don't know. He wasn't the commander-in-chief, but he was working up there in the command, and he was influential.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: So did he have any function in TO, Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that -- I don't know how to put it to you. He was -- shall we say, from the 6th of April, he was the most important person as the commander in the military department. But later, as those changes occurred, then a captain came, Vinko Pandurevic, he took over. But at the beginning, he was in charge. He was the main person who organised all these things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: And my last question, Mr. Vasiljevic, is: Who decided that you wouldn't be issued a weapon after being released from Uzamnica? Who decided on this?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He. He wouldn't give it to me. I handed it over to him, and he didn't give it to me again. I didn't want to go to the front line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: And you are the man who was in the army in your regular service --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would you, Your Honour, please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: You were a man who was in the army in the regular service. Wasn't it not normal for you, because you told us that you were issued this weapon against the signature. Didn't you ask, when you were deprived of your weapon, to have some declaration that you don't possess the weapon any more?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't give me anything. As I was saying when I spoke to him -- when I had to report to the command, I spoke to him. He took away my weapon, and he said, "You will go to prison." And I said, "Put me in prison. I won't eat." I went down to town an hour or two later, and then the military police came.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: I know this. I considered this quite normal that you were in detention and you were deprived of your weapon, but after you had this task of cleaning the street, you said you were afraid and the situation was dangerous. Why you were not issued the weapon again? Because after the return, you told us, from the hospital, you had these psychiatric problems and you were issued a weapon after that. So why this period you were without it? Can you explain this to me?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean before I went to hospital, while I was in Visegrad? I didn't quite understand you. You mean while I was in Visegrad why I didn't have a weapon, before I went to hospital? Is that what you're asking me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: I understood that when you were detained, you were deprived of your weapon. After you were released, you got this task to clean the street, but you said you had not your weapon back. So my question is -- I'm asking you for explanation, if you have any explanation why you were not issued with your weapon.

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't need a weapon any more. I was in town. I wasn't -- there was no need for it. I didn't insist that much. What was important for me was not to go to prison. I didn't need a weapon. I was in town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: When you were admitted to Uzice hospital as an emergency case, who explained the cause of your injury? It was you or someone else?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When they brought me by car to the hospital, they took me to the admission department. The driver gave these documents to those nurses, as is normal. He probably explained that it was a fracture. They X-rayed my leg. And there was a doctor on duty. His name was Dusko Jovicic. And that doctor who admits a patient, he treats him until the end. So I think that's how it goes. So the doctor who admits a patient to hospital. Of course, other doctors treat him as well, but the doctor who admits him to hospital, he is the person most responsible for the patient. So they X-rayed my leg, and they told me that both bones had been broken, though I knew that already in Visegrad when they X-rayed my leg, because Dr. Goran Loncarvic told me that already in Visegrad, that both bones had been broken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: No. My question is: Who explained the cause of your injury? That is you?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably the driver told them. I told the doctor whatever he asked me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The question, though, is: Did you explain to the doctor how the injury was caused? That's what Judge Taya is asking you.

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be quite honest, whether I actually explained to this particular doctor, Dusko Jovicic, myself, I can't recall. But later on, everyone knew. I told them. The patients knew. Now, to be quite honest, whether just then I told that doctor -- I don't even know whether he was present when the leg was X-rayed or was it being done by someone else, you know, specialists working with these machines, X-ray machines. So whether I had told him just then that I had fallen off a horse, I can't really remember. Maybe he didn't even asked me. He was just looking at the injury. So I'd rather not say that I did tell him just then. I really can't remember. If he asked me how the injury had occurred, then certainly I explained it to him. But they all knew that later on, everyone knew.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Can you remember what did you explain, how did you explain?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to tell you that I don't know whether I told him just then or whether he asked me just then. He just looked at the x-rays which he had, those from Visegrad. They did fresh x-rays. They established that there was a fracture, and he told me that both the bones had been broken. Now, whether I told him just then the cause, I just can't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: You didn't say that you fell on the flat surface in the battlefield?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't say that. As far as I understand, it says in the discharge paper "from the war zone of Visegrad." I think that's what they wrote for all the patients. Maybe it's because of the payment of hospital costs that this had to be indicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: You didn't mention the horse to the doctor?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying that I don't know whether I mentioned it just then, but later on everyone knew, the doctors knew. There was joking about it among the patients, and everybody, everybody knew.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Have you ever seen your case history which was prepared in Uzice hospital about you?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have anything except what it says on the discharge document, but what else the doctors write, they probably keep these records every day, so all the patient gets to know is what is written on the discharge document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Were you asked whether you were at work or out of work when you injured your leg?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think they asked me that. I don't know. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Were you asked also the day and hour of injury?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't ask me. They knew the day, because I was transferred on the same day from Visegrad to Uzice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: They could know when you arrived, but they could not know when the injury happened.

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the same day, I'm telling you, I was transferred from Visegrad to Uzice. If he asked me, "Today," I must have said, "Today, yes."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: You explained also your job?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't talk about that. No one asked me any questions about that. The doctor didn't ask me. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: You didn't say your job is reservist?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how they treated us. They know that, what is written in the discharge document, Territorial Defence. Yes, probably if he asked me, then I must have told him. I told him whatever he asked me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: I think that information, that is to say, whether you were at work or outside work on that day and hour of injury are essential to obtain health insurance; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: As to the witness list submitted by Defence counsel, did you consult with your Defence counsel before its submission?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean Defence witnesses, whether I consulted with my attorney 20 days ago or a month ago; is that what you're asking me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Whenever you have consulted with your Defence counsel. I don't know --

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't quite understand what you mean. When the attorney came to see me in February 2000 for the first time, when I decided that Mr. Domazet should be my Defence counsel, I told him that -- let me put it this way, when I gave my first statement, there was an officially-designated attorney from Foca, Slavisa, and I told him, too, that I had been in hospital. And then later, when Mr. Domazet came in February, I told him, "Vlado, you'll go to the hospital in Visegrad, the hospital in Uzice."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: 18 October 2001, Defence counsel submitted the list of witness. Before the submission of this list, you have consulted with Defence counsel?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether he should call those witnesses; is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: No. Who you want as a witness and the contents of the testimony of the witness, you have consulted with the Defence counsel?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the medical witnesses are concerned, I told him about Dr. Loncarevic in Visegrad, then I mentioned Moljevic and Jovicic, and the other witnesses applied themselves, the nurses and the neuropsychiatrist and the other physicians from the orthopaedic ward. They offered to come themselves because they watched it on television, they watched the witness statements and they, themselves, wanted to come.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: On that list, there is no name of Dr. Jovicevic who treated you as an emergency case, also Piresk [phoen] according to the case history of Uzice hospital. There is no name of Dr. Jovicevic. What is the reason why he is not called on the list of witnesses of Defence counsel?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I insisted with Mr. Domazet, but as far as I understand, the Defence counsel -- Mr. Jovicevic has to have his spine operated. Maybe Mr. Domazet can explain that. He is ill, he has problems with his spine and he has to undergo surgery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: On the same list, there are no names of Dr. Gordic, surgeon, and Dragana, nurse, who carried out the operation on 15th June 1992 according to the case history. What are the reasons why they are not called?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why. As regards the nurse, I know she was there and Gordic, who drilled my heel. I don't know whether Mr. Domazet spoke to them, but he can explain best. I just told him to go to the Uzice hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: After when you received outpatient treatment?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was orthopaedic department for 21 days. I explained they drilled my heel and put weights on, and at the end of those 21 days, they put my leg in a cast right up to my hip. Then I started walking with crutches, and they transferred me to the neuropsychiatric ward and I stayed there until the 28th of July, 1992 at the neuropsychiatry department.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: But after you left the Uzice hospital, you received treatment as an outpatient?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't have to stay in hospital. I went for the first time for the plaster to be shortened to below my knees; they call it a boot. And then when I went for a check-up the second time, the plaster was removed, and so when the doctors made an appointment for a check-up, I would get a document from Visegrad to go and see the specialist. I didn't have to go to the ward. There was a department on the ground floor where they work, and whichever doctor is on duty, he examines the patient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: What is the name of the specialist you mentioned just now?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the doctor who was on duty? Whoever is on duty, whoever is on duty that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: So it changes every time?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, usually. I think there are about -- I don't know how many exactly, there were five or six doctors working in the orthopaedic department, and I also had to go for check-ups to the neuropsychiatry department, and in that case, I did have to go to the actual ward upstairs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: You never broke your right leg; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Many witnesses gave testimony about some kind of certificate you wrote and handed over to (redacted). Even after those testimonies, you cannot remember about the certificate; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't have given him any kind of certificate. I was not a person who could issue any such official document. If I gave him anything, it could have been my telephone number or address or something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Then this is hypothetical question: A kind of certificate written by someone like you, if there were, and if it was shown to the police, it would guarantee the safety of people from Koritnik?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean if I would have given such a certificate. You're just asking me as an example. No. Who was I? The police has its own superiors, people in charge. They could just put me in prison if I were to issue any such certificates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: So according to you, such a certificate would never have such efficiency; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: My last series of questions concern your report on the Drina River incident to the police. You said that after the Drina River incident, you reported the crime committed by Milan Lukic and his group to Police Commander Tomic. That means that according to your understanding, the Drina River incident should be investigated by the police. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: That also means that if you happened to know the exact place where Milan Lukic was, you would inform the police or the investigation authority; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean if I knew where he lived?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would, of course. But I think they knew where he lived. They were living in Banja at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Such attitude of yours has not changed after the Drina River incident until today; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't understand what you mean. My behaviour hasn't changed? My attitude hasn't changed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Yes. If you know the exact place where Milan Lukic is, even today you would inform such information to the investigation authority?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to know. He's certainly in Serbia. There's no one who'd want him to be arrested more than me, because I'm being held responsible for his misdeeds. No one would be happier than me if he were arrested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: You said that in 1997 or 1998, you attended the baptism of the daughter of Milan Lukic. Where did that baptism take place?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Visegrad, in the church.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: You were informed about that baptism beforehand?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Milan Lukic also attended at that baptism?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Did you give that information to the police or SFOR stationed in Visegrad at that time?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police knew full well where he lived when he was released from prison in Belgrade and then transferred to Sarajevo and Kula. There was an apartment waiting for him in Visegrad and new furniture and everything, and he live there. They knew where he was. No one needed to explain it to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: French forces --

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. They gave him a coffee bar, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: The French forces of SFOR stationed in Visegrad at that time also knew?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean where he lived, whether they knew that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: No. Milan Lukic was at that time in Visegrad to attend at the baptism.

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. He was present at the christening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: No. My question is: The French force of SFOR stationed in Visegrad knew about the baptism that Milan Lukic attended?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether the French forces were in Visegrad just then. The French forces were there from June 1996. No. I'm sorry. Yes. From June 1999, 1999, and the baptism was in 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: No. The French forces were stationed there beforehand.

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, whether they knew, I don't know. I never had any contact with SFOR soldiers except those who were living at my place. They asked me whether they could live there and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: So you informed nothing to the police, neither to SFOR?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About the baptism, that he would attend the baptism? No. No. He was in Visegrad at the time. I don't know how to put it to you. He would come and go. He would be absent for two or three months, then he would come back for a couple of days. He moved around a lot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, do you want to ask any questions arising out of the Judges' questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, Judge Janu has inquired about an ID or identification papers. My question to you is: Would it be correct to say that if a person did not have their identification papers with them -- I'm sorry. Let me withdraw that. Would I be correct in saying that at the various checkpoints that were set up around Visegrad, that when a person would try to pass a checkpoint, they would be required to show their identification papers? Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know, sir. I never worked at those checkpoints. I never controlled anybody. I don't know. When the Uzice Corps were there, they were probably in control, and they didn't know the people. They probably controlled the Serbs, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, certainly at some point you, yourself, must have tried to pass a checkpoint. When you tried to pass the checkpoint, were you ever asked to show your identification papers?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you this: I had a checkpoint underneath my -- there was a checkpoint underneath my house when the Uzice Corps was there, and they never asked me for that. I lived there. I would make them a cup of coffee sometimes, to be frank.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did you ever see anybody at that checkpoint being asked to produce their identification papers?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They did stop a car, for example, going from Zupa. They controlled everyone, Serbs and Muslims alike. They would go into -- board a bus on one door, and the passengers would come out the other. They controlled everybody, checked everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And when they checked everybody, one of the things they would check would be the identification papers; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, personal documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So would it be correct to say that a person within Visegrad, attempting to leave Visegrad, would not be able to pass that checkpoint unless that person had their identification papers? Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably. Well, I don't know what they would do, how they would regulate this. I think all the inhabitants knew that they had to carry them with them. Well, somebody would guarantee for somebody if they knew them so that they could pass perhaps that way. That wouldn't be a problem either. I think that -- that's what I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You've also just told us now that regarding the police commander, Dragan Tomic, that you and him were good friends, that you trusted him and he trusted you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we were neighbours. We weren't that close. We were sort of the good friends. He -- in a neighbourly way. He was seven or eight -- he lived seven or eight houses away towards Visegrad. He was the chief of police or militia, as we called it. I knew him for years in that kind of way.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that other people in the area also knew about this relationship that you had with Dragan Tomic?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How do you mean? You mean were we great friends and did we go out together in times of peace? Or in cafes, did we frequent cafes? No. He had his own friends, his own circle of friends. That wasn't it. But we're good neighbours. That's our relationship, a good neighbourly relationship. Because I would pass by his house every day on my way to work, and I would stop if I was going by car. Or if he was going by car, he would take me in his car and drive me, give me a lift into town, that kind of thing, just like others would.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would I be correct in stating then that (redacted), who frequented your house, would have been aware that Dragan Tomic was a neighbour of yours?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. (redacted) knew him. He went by the same street. He knew that Dragan Tomic was a neighbour of mine. Mujo knew that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And Mujo also would have known that you and Dragan Tomic shared good neighbourly relations? Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I never said that. Let me say again. Let me tell you this, too: I was in Dragan Tomic's house for the first time perhaps in 1994 or 1995. And the first time I went was when his father died, actually. He never came to my house. He was never in my house, he or his brother, and I went to his house only when his father died. So we weren't close friends in any way. I want to explain that to you. We weren't friends like friends are, when you visit each other and so on, that close.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But you've told us that your relationship with Mr. Tomic was close enough that you trusted him with information that could have jeopardised both you and your family, correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So it was more than just an acquaintance. It was somebody who you trusted with the lives of yourself, your wife, and your children; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. That's his duty, because I trust you, too, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, would it be fair or would you agree with me that it would not be unreasonable for (redacted) to believe that if Dragan Tomic, as the commander of the police, became aware that you had written a letter or some kind of certificate ensuring the safety of Mujo and the other people, that Dragan Tomic would respect that and would not harm those people? Isn't that reasonable for Mujo to have believed that fact?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Had I written a certificate like that, Mujo had showed it when Milan Lukic came by, and Susnjar, the other man, and if it had been of any worth and valid, then I'm sure he would have shown it, had he had anything like that, but let me tell you, for me to issue any kind of certificate, that would not be any kind of authority for Tomic. He would criticise me and he would report me because it's not in my competence and authority to do so. How could I give anybody a piece of paper or anybody give anybody a piece of paper if he didn't have the authority to do so? All he could do was punish me for doing that. What's my paper worth? Nothing. He is in a position to issue a paper or the army or the competent authorities, some commander, some leader, some chief of some kind, somebody in charge of those people who is officially in charge of accompanying -- what would my paper mean, sir? My paper means nothing, who am I?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So let me ask you this question: So is it your testimony, and this is in some ways a hypothetical question like Judge Taya has asked you, if Mujo -- if Dragan Tomic had come to that house and spoken to (redacted) (redacted) had shown him a piece of paper signed by you, saying something to the effect that these people are okay, they should not be harmed, it's your testimony that Dragan Tomic would have come and punished you for having written that on a piece of paper? Is that your testimony here today?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he knows that those people are okay better than me. It's his duty to follow people and monitor them and to ensure that the police station has a command. If you gave a bad piece of paper, then you couldn't do that either. Now, a piece of paper, if it was something good, then there wouldn't be any grounds, but I don't know how to explain this to you or how to express myself. I don't know how to explain the thing to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I think you have, Mr. Vasiljevic. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Domazet, have you got any questions arising out of the questions of either of the Judges or Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Vasiljevic, you spoke about Drago Gavrilovic as a sort of a commander and sort of a high functionary or president of the SDS. Were you personally a member of the SDS or any political organisation at that time?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you exactly. That I was a member, no, I was not. Now, how do you explain when you vote for someone, when you vote for a party? Now, that I was a member or attended meetings at any time or any meeting, no, I did not. That wasn't -- I wasn't --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So you weren't a member of the SDS or any other political party, were you?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I didn't ask you who you voted for. When it comes to giving back weapons, the question was whether you received a certificate or piece of paper for returning the weapons, and you said no. Now, my question is: Were you issued a piece of paper when you were issued a weapon?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Was it customary for anybody handing in weapons or getting weapons to receive a certificate to that effect?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think the command takes that into account, the headquarters, the staff working at the headquarters sees to that, keeps records of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And if I understand you correctly, asked by the Judge about the incident at Sase, you said not only did you not point out the house which was opposite that place as being a Muslim house, but you claim that, in fact, it was a Serb house belonging to a man named Kosoric?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's the house belonging to Stojan Kosoric.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When we're talking about discharge papers and what it says in the different columns of the discharge sheet, one question was: Did you personally look to see when you left hospital, did you look at the document and did you pay attention to everything that is written -- was written in that document? Did you personally look at everything in the document?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I read the discharge paper, of course, several times but I didn't have it in my hands for years afterwards. It was in the archive and until you showed it to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When -- there was mention of insurance, some -- and we talked about insurance here today. There was a question raised about that. Now, in -- let's be more specific. Insurance can mean remuneration, you can receive remuneration for being injured, or it can also mean insurance, that is, the costs and expenses of medical treatment is paid by somebody for the treatment you receive. Now, my question is: Did you receive any remuneration and compensation for being injured and for being in hospital? Did you receive compensation of any kind?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I received no compensation for being treated in hospital or anything. How would I receive compensation? No, nobody asked me about that. And as far as insurance goes, well, the insurance, medical insurance goes via the TO, Territorial Defence. Now, I had got medical insurance from the company I worked for, and I don't know how this is regulated in wartime via the municipality or how it works.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You, personally, did you pay for the costs of the operation, the hospital costs and treatment?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you pay any costs at all?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And one more question connected to the question about Milan Lukic. If I understood from your answer, you say that he did not hide during the time he was in militia, he did not hide from the authorities in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't hide from the authorities. And in 1996, for example, he never went -- now, when he started to hide when the SFOR forces -- when the presence of the international police were stepped up, perhaps that was in 1988 and 1989 [as interpreted], then he didn't have the cafe any more and he began to hide then and change the places he was in. He changed his residence and so on, began to hide intensely after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Would you take a look at the transcript and look at the years. Is there a mistake there? It says 1988 and 1989. When you're talking about it, what year was it? What years are you thinking about when he started to hide, what years did you say?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1998 and 1999, I would change that. I said 1998 and 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you know whether Milan Lukic was accused, is there a secret indictment of The Hague Tribunal? Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that he was on an indictment, but I do know that he was in hiding, that he is in hiding. The papers wrote about that. The papers wrote about him. But I didn't know that there was an indictment against me in The Hague either, and I didn't like to associate with him because I expected him to be arrested. And even if I had to drink a cup of coffee, I would try to get away as soon as possible. Yes, I did know. I didn't know -- it wasn't only me who knew. The whole of Visegrad knew about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Vasiljevic. Thank you, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You may now return to your seat behind your counsel, Mr. Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, before the Defence -- the next Defence witness enters the courtroom, I should like to ask you to try and solve some problems with respect to the arrival of some witnesses and their testimony and the request made by some of them for protective measures in view of what they experienced in coming here, but I would like to discuss this in a private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Very well. We'll move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Domazet, is this one of the witnesses for whom we've made an order for protective measures?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sir, would you please make the solemn declaration in terms of the document that is being handed to you by the court officer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sit down, please, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: It will be Mr. Tanaskovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tanaskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TANASKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dikic, good morning.

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA DIKIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TANASKOVIC
utterances.text: I hope you feel better now after the unpleasantness and the provocations you were exposed to on your journey to The Hague and that you're able to testify today.

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA DIKIC
utterances.text: I am. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TANASKOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us your name, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA DIKIC
utterances.text: Dragisa Dikic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TANASKOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us when and where you were born.

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA DIKIC
utterances.text: On the 13th of September, 1948, in Loznica near Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. TANASKOVIC
utterances.text: And where do you reside?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA DIKIC
utterances.text: I am living now in Vojvode Stepe Street, no number, in Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. TANASKOVIC
utterances.text: Since when have you been living there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA DIKIC
utterances.text: I've been living in that street, or, rather, my parents have been living there for more than 40 years, and I have been there all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TANASKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please make a pause between my questions, and answers so that the interpreters have time to interpret. And you can look at the transcript on your monitor, if it's switched on, to be able to follow. Tell me, what is your profession?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA DIKIC
utterances.text: By profession, I am an auto mechanic and bodyworker.

utterances.speaker: MR. TANASKOVIC
utterances.text: Are you married?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA DIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TANASKOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, what is your occupation now?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA DIKIC
utterances.text: I am practising the same trade, as a mechanic and a bodyworker.

utterances.speaker: MR. TANASKOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that you have your privately-owned business?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA DIKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I have had that private business for some 30 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. TANASKOVIC
utterances.text: So that means that that was your occupation before the war as well?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA DIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TANASKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know Mr. Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA DIKIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TANASKOVIC
utterances.text: Where did you meet him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA DIKIC
utterances.text: He's my neighbour, Mr. Vasiljevic is. He lives about 100 or 150 metres away from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TANASKOVIC
utterances.text: For how long has the Vasiljevic family been living in your neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA DIKIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you, sir, I don't know exactly since when the Vasiljevic family has been living there, but roughly as far as I am able to remember, for some 20 years and more.

utterances.speaker: MR. TANASKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know Mr. Vasiljevic prior to that 20-year period? Please wait a moment before giving your answer.

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA DIKIC
utterances.text: I have known Vasiljevic ever since he started working as a waiter. I am unable to tell you how long that is exactly, but it's been a long time, many years that we've known each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. TANASKOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that you know him as a waiter, do you know where he worked as a waiter?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA DIKIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, he worked throughout in the catering establishment called Panos of Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. TANASKOVIC
utterances.text: Does that company have several catering establishments?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA DIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TANASKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know in which of those establishments Mr. Vasiljevic worked?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA DIKIC
utterances.text: I think that Vasiljevic worked in all the different establishments, at least those I am familiar with: The Visegrad Hotel, the old Panos, the Visegrad Banja Ospar [phoen]. He probably worked at Bikavac well, but I can't remember with precision.

utterances.speaker: MR. TANASKOVIC
utterances.text: As neighbours, would you see Mr. Vasiljevic frequently and his family?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA DIKIC
utterances.text: Well, virtually every day, especially more recently because I have a workshop which is on the road itself so that I see everyone as they pass by.

utterances.speaker: MR. TANASKOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, where were you during the war?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA DIKIC
utterances.text: During the war, I was mobilised to the Territorial Defence or as -- by the military. I was assigned to the workshop for the maintenance of vehicles, and that is where I spent the whole war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TANASKOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that you were deployed there, assigned to that position by the TO or the military?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA DIKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was assigned there. I got a call-up, and that was my assignment. Before, it was called the JNA, then it was the TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. TANASKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us where that workshop was to which you were assigned?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA DIKIC
utterances.text: The workshop was on the bus station, at the bus station slightly outside town. It was the workshop owned by the company Centrotrans, and that is where we worked all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TANASKOVIC
utterances.text: When you mentioned Centrotrans, what was the area of activity of that company?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA DIKIC
utterances.text: Centrotrans was a company for the transport of passengers, and they had a department for technical examinations of vehicles, and it was that department that was used for the maintenance of vehicles where I worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. TANASKOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to you, were there other mechanics and workers in that workshop?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA DIKIC
utterances.text: I had three other colleagues of mine working with me and a boss, a superior, and then there were other services like locksmiths and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. TANASKOVIC
utterances.text: Whose vehicles did you repair?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA DIKIC
utterances.text: We repaired the vehicles of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TANASKOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that this workshop had any kind of special security measures, that everyone could not freely go in as they wished?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA DIKIC
utterances.text: The workshop had a number of vehicles, I don't know the exact number. There was a barrier. There was an office, a guard who would let the vehicles in. Because all vehicles could not come in, those that were not in the possession of the Territorial Defence or the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TANASKOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you were assigned to this workshop. My next question is: Did you go home at all?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA DIKIC
utterances.text: We were accommodated on the upper floor of the same building where the workshop was, that is where we slept. But I went home quite often because I was able to go in a car to visit my family and to come back.

utterances.speaker: MR. TANASKOVIC
utterances.text: When you went home, would you see Mr. Vasiljevic then, too?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA DIKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TANASKOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, do you know whether he had any assignment and what it was, if you know?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA DIKIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you who was assigned where, but I would see Vasiljevic quite frequently in the street with a small group of men cleaning the town. That's what I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. TANASKOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that you would see Vasiljevic frequently, did you notice that he had a weapon on him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA DIKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TANASKOVIC
utterances.text: When you would see him in the street cleaning, can you remember how he was dressed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA DIKIC
utterances.text: I can remember because whenever I saw him in the street, he was wearing civilian clothes. I remember that well because I always wore my own clothes, so actually I hardly had any clothes at all at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TANASKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember, try to remember - I know it's difficult - what colour those civilian clothes were?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA DIKIC
utterances.text: I just know that he always wore, as he always did for as long as I've known him, dark coloured suits like I wear, not light coloured. So he wasn't that conspicuous. I can't remember the colour exactly, but I know they were not light colours, but dark colours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TANASKOVIC
utterances.text: When you said a moment ago that you would see him cleaning the town, tell me what the town was being cleaned of, and did Vasiljevic do this alone or with others?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA DIKIC
utterances.text: The town was cleaned of various rubbish thrown by people out into the street, so it was really very dirty. I would clean, too. Then there were shopkeepers who would clean in front of their own shops, and Vasiljevic would lead this group of five or six men, I think there were, to clean, and they removed the rubbish. There were some larger objects, too. I don't know. People were throwing out all kinds of things into the street.

utterances.speaker: MR. TANASKOVIC
utterances.text: In your opinion, was the town clean after the cleaning began to be organised?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA DIKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was clean. It couldn't be absolutely a hundred per cent in order, but if it hadn't been for this cleaning, one couldn't pass, walk along the street properly. And I drove the car a lot, and I was able to notice it. And somebody had to do that work.

utterances.speaker: MR. TANASKOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, who was working with Vasiljevic on the cleaning job?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA DIKIC
utterances.text: Doing the cleaning, as far as I noticed, there were men of other ethnic groups. There were Serbs and Muslims, shopkeepers. Salesmen would also clean, probably under his kind of orders or requests. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TANASKOVIC
utterances.text: A moment ago, you said that he wore a civilian dark suit or clothes, as you put it. Tell us, please, when you saw him cleaning the town or organising the cleaning, did you notice him wearing anything on those clothes? Wait a moment, please. Don't hurry.

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA DIKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. On his arm, he had a red ribbon, only I can't remember exactly which arm.

utterances.speaker: MR. TANASKOVIC
utterances.text: On that ribbon, was there any sign or emblem, or was it just a red ribbon, plain red ribbon?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA DIKIC
utterances.text: A red ribbon, an ordinary red ribbon of -- made of some material, cloth.

utterances.speaker: MR. TANASKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dikic, can you tell us, when you would see him involved in the organisation of the cleaning of the town, what period was that? What time period?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA DIKIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly the time, but he cleaned the town. From the beginning of the war, as far as I remember, he was involved in the cleaning of the town. I don't know the exact dates. I wasn't aware that I would ever need to remember those things.

utterances.speaker: MR. TANASKOVIC
utterances.text: If you could tell us, was that before the Uzice Corps arrived or after they had left?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA DIKIC
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly when that cleaning took place. He didn't just clean the town on one day for me to be able to remember the day. I just know that I saw him many times cleaning the town. I think it could have been after the Uzice Corps left and also before they left.

utterances.speaker: MR. TANASKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember when the Uzice Corps arrived or when they left? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA DIKIC
utterances.text: Again, I can't tell you the exact date, but I think that the corps was there in May. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TANASKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see Mr. Vasiljevic after that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA DIKIC
utterances.text: I did see him, but again I can't give you any exact date. I saw him on crutches, but again I can't tell you when exactly that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TANASKOVIC
utterances.text: When you saw him carrying crutches, where would you see him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA DIKIC
utterances.text: Also in passing, because as I was saying, I used the car a lot, so that as I drove by, I would see him going walking with crutches.

utterances.speaker: MR. TANASKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know or did you learn why he was using crutches?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA DIKIC
utterances.text: I did. As according to what I heard - I didn't see it - he fell off a horse, and he broke a leg.

utterances.speaker: MR. TANASKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know or do you not know for how long he used those crutches?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA DIKIC
utterances.text: For a couple of months he did, but again, I can't tell you any exact dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. TANASKOVIC
utterances.text: You told us you knew your neighbour Vasiljevic well. Tell me, did he ever wear a moustache?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA DIKIC
utterances.text: No. I don't remember ever seeing him with a moustache.

utterances.speaker: MR. TANASKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether he had a nickname?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA DIKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TANASKOVIC
utterances.text: You said that Mr. Vasiljevic worked as a waiter and also he was your neighbour. Tell us, please, do you know that Vasiljevic liked to have a drink and that he got drunk quite often?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA DIKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know that. He liked to have a drink.

utterances.speaker: MR. TANASKOVIC
utterances.text: And where would that usually be?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA DIKIC
utterances.text: Usually in the -- in the restaurants he was working in, in Panos or in Cadzava, in Mezalin. In those coffee bars which were not too crowded.

utterances.speaker: MR. TANASKOVIC
utterances.text: So I can take it that you would see him drunk?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA DIKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I would see him under the influence of alcohol, drunk.

utterances.speaker: MR. TANASKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how he behaved when he was under the influence of alcohol? Was he aggressive or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA DIKIC
utterances.text: I would see him drunk many times. He's funny. He becomes funny. As far as I know him, he was never aggressive, nor did I ever see him provoking a quarrel or a conflict. He wasn't very interesting when he was drunk.

utterances.speaker: MR. TANASKOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that in that condition, in your opinion, he would not cause any excesses?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA DIKIC
utterances.text: As far as I know and the many times that I was present, he did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TANASKOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, did you ever see Mr. Vasiljevic wearing a uniform? And if you did, what kind of uniform?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Haven't you already asked him that question? I thought you asked him that a long time ago, and he said no, he'd never seen him in a uniform. I don't know whether -- I'm sorry. I'm reminded it might have been a cleaning uniform. You're asking now about an army uniform, are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. TANASKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TANASKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you answer that question, Mr. Dikic, please?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA DIKIC
utterances.text: I don't remember seeing him wearing a uniform. And to be a hundred per cent truthful, it's possible that I may have seen him wearing an SMB shirt. That is an olive-green coloured shirt, the shirt worn by our former army. Actually, it still exists. It is the colour of military uniforms. But as for any other part of the uniform, I really never saw him wearing anything but civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TANASKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, in your street, your street and Mr. Vasiljevic's street, was there a checkpoint, and if so, when, if you can tell us?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA DIKIC
utterances.text: There was a checkpoint. Actually, between his house and mine, in fact closer to his house than mine. It was a military checkpoint manned by the Uzice Corps, and I think that it existed, and I apologise again if I give you the wrong date, but when the Uzice Corps arrived at the beginning, so this may have been April or May, end of April. I don't know exactly. When the Uzice Corps entered, they immediately set up this checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. TANASKOVIC
